deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a continuation of Riemann's natural-philosophical notes on the external conditions of the life process (Nat. Ph. pp. 29-31). The argument runs as follows.

(i) It finishes the list of facts illustrating thesis 1 from p. 29: the more highly developed a life process is, the more its bearers must be shielded from external causes that change the relative position of their parts. Item 3: the parts of the nervous system that serve independent thought are protected as well as possible against all these influences, i.e. mechanical forces, temperature changes and light.

(ii) Explanation of thesis 1. The relative position of the parts can be determined by processes in the interior of matter only to the extent that it is not determined by external causes of motion. Riemann then adds a strong further claim: such independence from external causes holds inside the Earth's crust ('innerhalb der Erdrinde') to a far higher degree than any organic arrangement outside the crust could achieve. The implicit suggestion (my reading) is that the most perfect seat of a 'thought/life process' would be the Earth's interior rather than surface organisms. This fits the Fechner-influenced speculation, known from his published philosophical fragments, about a soul of the Earth.

(iii) Apparent objection. Facts 4 and 5 of p. 29 seem to contradict this. Fact 4: only the four 'organic' elements C, H, N, O carry life. Fact 5: organic compounds exist only within certain temperature limits. They would contradict it if these observed conditions held absolutely rather than only relative to our range of experience.

(iv) Two arguments against absolute validity:
(1) Otherwise all of nature except the Earth's surface would be dead, since on all other celestial bodies the heat and pressure conditions would destroy organic compounds.
(2) It is 'absurd' (ungereimt) that the organic arose from the inorganic on the solidified crust. To explain the origin of the lowest organisms one must already assume an organizing principle, i.e. a thought (life) process, under conditions in which organic compounds could not exist.

(v) Conclusion. These conditions hold only for the life process under present conditions on the Earth's surface. Only insofar as we can explain them can we draw conclusions valid under other conditions, that is, judge whether life is possible elsewhere.

(vi) Transition to p. 31: why are the four organic elements the general bearers of life? The next page answers via their difficulty of condensation, which leads into Riemann's molecular hypothesis of thermal and chemical repulsion versus capillary forces.
errors: No mathematical errors, because there is no mathematics on the page.

Argument (1) rests on an empirical overgeneralization. Riemann claims that on all other celestial bodies heat and pressure conditions preclude organic compounds. This was unknowable then and is incorrect by modern standards for some bodies.

Argument (2) is a vitalist premise, not a derivation. It asserts as 'absurd' that the organic arose from the inorganic. This stands against Wöhler's 1828 urea synthesis and against modern abiogenesis research.
Unsupported step: the claim that the Earth's interior provides greater independence from external causes of motion than any organic arrangement is asserted without justification.

results.what: Speculative argument that observed conditions for life (C,H,N,O; temperature limits) are only relative to Earth's surface, so life/'thought processes' may exist under other conditions (Earth's interior, other celestial bodies)
results.modern_name: Vitalist / panpsychist natural philosophy (Fechner-style); a precursor of 'life under other conditions' speculation
results.usually_credited_to: G. T. Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) and the Naturphilosophie tradition

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely qualitative natural philosophy with no mathematical content. Riemann's Fechner-influenced speculations on the soul, the Earth and life are already known in part from the philosophical fragments published in his Werke. This particular passage may be unpublished, but it adds nothing of mathematical or scientific priority.
transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'Theil[-..-]' is 'Theile' with a few struck-out letters following 'Theil'. The intended reading is 'der Theile'.
There is a marginal brace/bracket to the right of argument '1, Man müßte alsdann ...' that the transcription does not note.
The overall transcription matches the image well. Readings such as 'Erdrinde', 'ungereimt', 'organisirendes Princip' and 'Denk- (Lebens-) Proceß' are confirmed.
